passage: Science note, Rashmi, Class 3. I gave the class forty animal cards to sort. Most groups made "land" and "water" piles. Raghav, eight, did something different. He made "animals with backbones" first, then split it into birds, fish, mammals and reptiles. Under mammals he made a small pile of "mammals that live in water" and put the whale and the dolphin there. When a classmate said, "Whale is a fish," Raghav said, "It's in the water pile and the mammal pile. It can be in both." Tomorrow I will draw a big tree diagram on the board using his groups.

qa.q: Which animals did Raghav put in "mammals that live in water"?
qa.a: The whale and the dolphin.

qa.q: What does "It can be in both" show about how Raghav was thinking?
qa.a: He understood that one animal can sit in a smaller group inside a bigger one and still share a trait with another group.

qa.q: How will Rashmi's tree diagram help the class?
qa.a: It shows groups inside groups clearly, so other children can see the levels Raghav used.

qa.q: How might the classmate who said "Whale is a fish" feel?
qa.a: A little corrected, but the idea of it being in both piles gives an easy way to change their mind.

grounding: It shows a child sorting animals into groups with subgroups inside them and seeing overlapping sets.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Spent the whole afternoon sorting my stamp collection. First I had them by colour, which looked pretty but made no sense. Then I did countries, but some countries had only one stamp. Finally I made big groups by continent, smaller groups by country inside each, and inside India, groups by what's on them: birds, freedom fighters, trains. Yash asked why the Kenya giraffe wasn't with my India peacock, since both are animals. I said, "It's Africa first, then animals." He said I could do animals first. Annoyingly, he's right. Both work.
- Harsha

qa.q: How did Harsha first sort the stamps?
qa.a: By colour.

qa.q: Why did Harsha write "Annoyingly, he's right"?
qa.a: Harsha felt a bit irritated that Yash had a good point, but was honest enough to admit there is more than one way to sort.

qa.q: What could Harsha try to keep both kinds of sorting?
qa.a: Make a separate list or small labels, so a stamp can be found either by continent or by what is pictured on it.

qa.q: How does Yash see the collection differently?
qa.a: He thinks of subject first, so for him the giraffe and the peacock belong together as animals.

grounding: It shows a child building a nested classification of stamps and realising a different hierarchy also works.

passage: Madhuri Pishi's shop in their small town was a jumble: soap next to lentils, biscuits under the brooms. On a holiday, Bidisha, ten, took charge. "First, things you eat and things you don't." Two big piles. Then she split the food: grains, dals, spices, snacks. Then the dals: moong, masoor, chana, each in its own tin with a paper label. When a customer asked for masoor, Pishi found it in a second. "How did you think of it?" she asked. Bidisha shrugged. "Big box, smaller boxes inside, smallest inside those."

qa.q: What were Bidisha's first two piles?
qa.a: Things you eat and things you don't.

qa.q: What does Bidisha's shrug suggest about how she saw her system?
qa.a: It seemed natural and obvious to her, and she felt confident enough to take charge on her own.

qa.q: How could Pishi keep the system working?
qa.a: Keep the labels and ask Bidisha to add new items into the right group, so the order lasts.

qa.q: How might a customer experience the new shop?
qa.a: They get served faster, since Pishi finds things in a second instead of searching the jumble.

grounding: It shows a girl organising a shop into categories, subcategories and smaller sets within them.

passage: In the flat above a bakery in Lisbon, Emeka and Tomas tipped out their sticker collection. 'Animals and not-animals,' Tomas said. They made two heaps. Then Emeka split the animals: 'Birds, fish, mammals.' Tomas held up a penguin. 'Bird, even though it swims.' Emeka nodded, then made smaller piles inside mammals: cats, dogs, bears. 'Look, lions go in cats, and cats go in mammals, and mammals go in animals.' Tomas drew boxes inside boxes on a page. 'It's like Russian dolls!'

qa.q: Where did Tomas put the penguin?
qa.a: Tomas put it with the birds, even though it swims.

qa.q: What does Tomas drawing boxes inside boxes suggest about Tomas's thinking?
qa.a: It suggests Tomas felt excited at grasping that groups fit inside bigger groups, and wanted to picture it clearly.

qa.q: How could Emeka and Tomas extend this sorting activity?
qa.a: They could try the same boxes-in-boxes method with other things, like foods or vehicles.

qa.q: How might a younger child see the sticker heaps?
qa.a: A younger child might just sort by colour or favourite, without seeing that groups sit inside larger groups.

grounding: Illustrates children organising items into nested hierarchies of sets and subsets, set in Portugal.

passage: The school library had a pile of returned books, and Ira, the librarian, asked Jahnavi to help. Jahnavi split them into Fiction and Non-fiction. Then, inside Non-fiction, she made Science, History and Sport. Inside Science she noticed some were about space, some about animals. 'Ma'am, can I make a space shelf inside the science shelf?' Ira laughed. 'Show me.' Jahnavi drew a chart: Books → Non-fiction → Science → Space. 'So every space book is a science book, but not every science book is about space.'

qa.q: How did Jahnavi first split the pile of books?
qa.a: She split them into Fiction and Non-fiction.

qa.q: Why was Jahnavi excited to make a space shelf?
qa.a: She felt eager to organise the books more precisely and was pleased at spotting a group within a group.

qa.q: How could Ira use Jahnavi's chart?
qa.a: She could put it up in the library so other students learn to find books through these nested groups.

qa.q: How might other students benefit from Jahnavi's sorting?
qa.a: They could find books faster, especially if they are looking for a specific topic like space.

grounding: Shows a child organising library books into sets and subsets, in a school setting.

passage: I'm Keerthana, and I help in the school library on Fridays. Last week Elizabeth, from my class, offered to sort the returned books. She didn't just stack them. She made two piles, stories and facts. Then she split the facts into animals, space and history, and inside animals she made birds and fish. She even had a sticky note that said "Sharks: fish, not whales!" She looked so focused I didn't disturb her. I don't know why she enjoyed it, but she finished the whole trolley.

qa.q: What were the first two piles Elizabeth made?
qa.a: Stories and facts.

qa.q: What might Elizabeth have been feeling as she sorted the books?
qa.a: She seemed absorbed and satisfied, enjoying making order out of the pile.

qa.q: How could the librarian build on Elizabeth's sorting skills?
qa.a: Ask her to help label the shelves by groups and smaller groups, so others can find books.

qa.q: How does Keerthana see Elizabeth's work?
qa.a: Keerthana is impressed by how carefully it was done, though not sure why Elizabeth enjoyed it.

grounding: Shows a child sorting library books into groups and subgroups, seen by a classmate.

passage: First weekend: Avni, nine, dumped her beach shells on the floor and sorted them by colour: white, pink, brown. Her cousin Kiran said, "But these two are the same kind." Second weekend: Avni sorted them again, this time into spiral shells and fan shells. Third weekend: she had a shoebox with two sections, and inside the fan section, little bags for big and small. "All shells, then two kinds, then sizes," she explained to Kiran. He nodded slowly.

qa.q: How did Avni first sort her shells?
qa.a: By colour: white, pink, brown.

qa.q: How might Avni have felt when she showed Kiran her shoebox?
qa.a: She probably felt proud and satisfied with her new, more complex system.

qa.q: What helped Avni move to a better system?
qa.a: Kiran's comment pushed her to notice kinds instead of colours, and she kept trying over the weeks.

qa.q: How might Kiran see the final shoebox?
qa.a: He seems impressed and is still working out the idea of groups inside groups.

grounding: Shows a child moving from simple colour sorting to nested groups and subgroups over three weekends.

passage: "Listen, beta. When I, your Anirban Dadu, was ten, my father ran a spice shop, and one monsoon he said, 'Sort the jars.' I lined them up by colour first, red, yellow, brown. My sister Tanuja laughed. 'Chilli and turmeric are both powders, and pepper and cumin are seeds.' So I started again. Powders on one shelf, seeds on another. Then, inside seeds, whole ones and crushed. Father came back, opened his mouth to scold, then looked closer and said nothing. The next day he let me write the labels."

qa.q: How did Anirban first line up the jars?
qa.a: By colour first, red, yellow, brown.

qa.q: What might young Anirban have felt when his father looked closer and said nothing?
qa.a: He was probably nervous at first, then quietly proud when his father let him write the labels.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Anirban sorted?
qa.a: Tanuja pointing out powders and seeds made him start again with groups inside groups.

qa.q: How might Tanuja have felt when her little brother used her idea?
qa.a: She might feel pleased and a bit proud, even if she had laughed at first.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a child he learned to sort spice jars into groups and subgroups.

passage: The school library closed in fifteen minutes, and a whole box of donated books sat on the table. Sunaina Ma'am, the librarian, sighed. "Farhan, can you sort these?" Farhan, eleven, made piles fast: stories, facts, poems. Then he looked at the facts pile. "Animals, space, machines." He split the animals again: mammals, birds, fish. "And cats go under mammals," he muttered, sliding one book to the side. The bell rang. Sunaina Ma'am looked at the neat stacks and raised her eyebrows. "You made a family tree for books."

qa.q: How many minutes until the library closed?
qa.a: Fifteen minutes.

qa.q: How can you tell Farhan felt focused while sorting?
qa.a: He worked fast, muttered to himself and kept splitting piles into smaller groups.

qa.q: What could Sunaina Ma'am ask Farhan to try next?
qa.a: She could ask him to make labels for each group so others can find the books easily.

qa.q: How does Sunaina Ma'am see Farhan's sorting?
qa.a: She is impressed and surprised, comparing it to a family tree.

grounding: Under time pressure, a boy sorts library books into groups and sub-groups.

passage: Wasim's father, Rafiq, ran a small shop in the Mumbra market. On Sunday, he handed Wasim a sack of mixed packets. "Put these on the shelves properly." Wasim, ten, stared at the heap. Then he started: grains on the top shelf, pulses in the middle, spices on the bottom. He paused over a packet of moong. "Pulses... but whole moong and split moong go next to each other, then the dals." He made little rows inside each shelf. Rafiq looked up from the counter. "Why like that?" "So people can find the small kinds inside the big kinds," Wasim said.

qa.q: What went on the top shelf?
qa.a: Grains.

qa.q: What does Wasim's pause over the packet of moong suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was thinking hard and curious about how to fit the packet into the right sub-group.

qa.q: How could Rafiq encourage Wasim's sorting?
qa.a: He could ask Wasim to label each shelf and sub-group so customers can find items easily.

qa.q: How might Rafiq see Wasim's way of arranging the shelves?
qa.a: He seems curious and perhaps impressed by his son's logical grouping.

grounding: A boy arranges shop items into categories and subcategories.

passage:
"I'm thinking of something," said Tejas. "Guess."
"Is it alive?" Tarun asked.
"Yes."
"Is it an animal?"
"Yes."
"Is it a mammal?"
"No."
"Bird?"
"Yes."
"Hmm. Can it fly?"
"No!"
Tarun counted on his fingers. "Birds that can't fly... ostrich, emu, penguin."
"Warm!"
"Does it live where it's cold?"
"Yes!"
"Penguin!"
Tejas groaned. "How did you get it so fast?"
"Big group first, then smaller. Animals, birds, birds that don't fly, cold ones." Tarun grinned. "Your turn to guess mine."

qa.q: What was Tejas thinking of?
qa.a: A penguin.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel as he narrowed down the guesses?
qa.a: Tarun felt confident and pleased, grinning after solving it so quickly.

qa.q: Which strategy helped Tarun win, and when else could it help?
qa.a: Starting with big groups and narrowing to smaller ones; it could help when sorting things or looking something up.

qa.q: What is it like for Tejas when Tarun guesses so fast?
qa.a: Tejas feels surprised and a bit frustrated, groaning at losing so quickly, and may pick something harder next time.

grounding: Two boys play a guessing game where one narrows from big categories down to subsets.

passage:
When I was eleven, I had a huge pile of animal cards. Chinmay and I kept swapping them, and they were a mess.

One Sunday I decided to sort them. First into animals and birds. Then the animals into wild and pet. Then the wild ones into cats, dogs, bears. I made little boxes with labels.

Chinmay laughed. "Why is the tiger in two boxes?"

"It's not. It's in 'cats', and 'cats' is inside 'wild'."

He didn't get it at first. I drew a big circle with smaller circles inside.

I'm Samir, and that was the first time I understood that one group can live inside another.

qa.q: How did Samir first sort the cards?
qa.a: First into animals and birds.

qa.q: How did Samir feel explaining the circles to Chinmay?
qa.a: Samir felt proud and determined to make Chinmay understand.

qa.q: How could a teacher build on Samir's sorting?
qa.a: A teacher could give him more things to sort into groups and subgroups and ask him to draw them.

qa.q: How might Chinmay see the sorting at first?
qa.a: Chinmay found it confusing and funny at first, asking why the tiger was in two boxes.

grounding: A child looks back on sorting animal cards into groups and subgroups and understanding sets within sets.

passage:
Nature walk note, monsoon term.

On today's walk, Vinita, ten, collected leaves, stones and insects in her box. At the shelter, she sorted them without being asked: living and non-living, then living into plants and animals, then animals into insects and snails.

When a friend put a beetle with the stones, Vinita said, "It's alive, so it goes in the animal group, then in insects."

I'll set up a sorting table in class next week. — Ujjwal

qa.q: How did Vinita first sort her collection?
qa.a: She sorted it into living and non-living.

qa.q: How might Vinita have felt when she corrected her friend?
qa.a: Vinita was likely confident and eager to share her sorting.

qa.q: How is Ujjwal planning to support Vinita's classification skills?
qa.a: Ujjwal will set up a sorting table in class next week.

qa.q: How might Vinita's friend feel being corrected?
qa.a: The friend might feel a bit embarrassed but also curious to learn.

grounding: A nature walk note records a child sorting collections into groups and subgroups.

passage:
Eid holidays, Thursday

Sudha and I sorted Nana's bookshelf today. It was a total mess.

First we made two piles: stories and not-stories. Then the stories into Urdu and English. Then the not-stories into science, history and cooking.

Sudha said the cooking books should go with science, because cooking is chemistry. We argued for ten minutes. We gave cooking its own little shelf inside "not-stories".

Nana came in and couldn't find his newspaper. But he found his old poetry book, which he hadn't seen for years.

Wasim

qa.q: How did Wasim and Sudha first sort the books?
qa.a: First they made two piles: stories and not-stories.

qa.q: How did Nana feel when he found his poetry book?
qa.a: Nana was probably delighted and surprised, finding a book he hadn't seen for years.

qa.q: How did Wasim and Sudha solve their disagreement about cooking books?
qa.a: They gave cooking its own little shelf inside "not-stories".

qa.q: How might Sudha feel about the argument over cooking books?
qa.a: Sudha might feel satisfied that the idea about cooking was taken seriously.

grounding: During the Eid holidays, a child sorts a bookshelf into groups and subgroups with a cousin.

passage: It was harvest time in their village near Hoshangabad, and Dadaji's small grain shop was piled with sacks. Seema and her cousin Ritu were told to label the tins. Ritu wrote "rice", "wheat", "moong", "masoor" and "chana" and lined them up in a row. Seema frowned. "Rice and wheat are grains. Moong, masoor and chana are dals. And all of them are food we sell." On the slate she drew a big circle marked FOOD, and inside it two smaller circles, GRAINS and DALS. Dadaji peered over his glasses. "And where do moong sprouts go?" Seema thought. "Inside dals, in a smaller circle." Ritu clapped.

qa.q: What did Seema write in the big circle on the slate?
qa.a: She marked the big circle FOOD.

qa.q: Why did Seema frown at Ritu's row of labels?
qa.a: She was dissatisfied because the row didn't show how the items belonged together, and she wanted a clearer order.

qa.q: How could Dadaji use Seema's circles in the shop?
qa.a: He could arrange the shelves by the same groups, grains on one side and dals on the other, so customers find things quickly.

qa.q: What is it like for Ritu to see Seema's circles?
qa.a: Ritu is impressed and delighted, clapping when Seema fits the sprouts into a smaller circle.

grounding: Shows a child organising shop goods into groups within groups during harvest time.
